claim: Neurovascular coupling is a critical brain mechanism whereby changes to blood flow accompany localised neural activity.
source: Neurovascular coupling is a critical brain mechanism whereby changes to blood flow accompany localised neural activity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neurovascular coupling.

claim: The breakdown of neurovascular coupling is linked to the development and progression of several neurological conditions including dementia.
source: The breakdown of neurovascular coupling is linked to the development and progression of several neurological conditions including dementia.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about neurovascular coupling and neurological disease.

claim: Atherosclerosis in mouse models is characterized by significantly reduced blood volume.
source: We report novel findings with atherosclerosis where neurovascular decline is characterised by significantly reduced blood volume, altered levels of oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, in addition to global neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reduced HbT in PCSK9-ATH mice.

claim: Atherosclerosis in mouse models is characterized by altered levels of oxyhaemoglobin.
source: We report novel findings with atherosclerosis where neurovascular decline is characterised by significantly reduced blood volume, altered levels of oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, in addition to global neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing altered HbO levels in PCSK9-ATH mice.

claim: Atherosclerosis in mouse models is characterized by altered levels of deoxyhaemoglobin.
source: We report novel findings with atherosclerosis where neurovascular decline is characterised by significantly reduced blood volume, altered levels of oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, in addition to global neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing altered HbR levels in PCSK9-ATH mice.

claim: Atherosclerosis in mouse models is characterized by global neuroinflammation.

evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased inflammatory markers in PCSK9-ATH mice.

claim: In the comorbid mixed model (J20-PCSK9-MIX), there is a 3x increase in hippocampal amyloid-beta plaques.
source: In the comorbid mixed model (J20-PCSK9-MIX), we report a 3 x increase in hippocampal amyloid-beta plaques.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased Aβ plaques in J20-PCSK9-MIX mice.

claim: Cortical spreading depression due to electrode insertion into the brain was worse in diseased animals.
source: A key finding was that cortical spreading depression (CSD) due to electrode insertion into the brain was worse in the diseased animals and led to a prolonged period of hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing more severe CSD in diseased mouse models.

claim: Cortical spreading depression in diseased animals led to a prolonged period of hypoxia.
source: A key finding was that cortical spreading depression (CSD) due to electrode insertion into the brain was worse in the diseased animals and led to a prolonged period of hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing prolonged reductions in HbT and HbO following CSD.

claim: Systemic atherosclerosis can be detrimental to neurovascular health.
source: These findings suggest that systemic atherosclerosis can be detrimental to neurovascular health and that having cardiovascular comorbidities can exacerbate pre-existing Alzheimer's-related amyloid-plaques.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing neurovascular decline in PCSK9-ATH mice.

claim: Having cardiovascular comorbidities can exacerbate pre-existing Alzheimer's-related amyloid-plaques.
source: These findings suggest that systemic atherosclerosis can be detrimental to neurovascular health and that having cardiovascular comorbidities can exacerbate pre-existing Alzheimer's-related amyloid-plaques.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental finding of increased Aβ plaques in the mixed model.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia worldwide.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia worldwide, with the vast majority of cases being sporadic and occurring at age 65 years and over.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Alzheimer's disease epidemiology.

claim: The vast majority of Alzheimer's disease cases are sporadic and occur at age 65 years and over.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia worldwide, with the vast majority of cases being sporadic and occurring at age 65 years and over.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Alzheimer's disease epidemiology.

claim: AD and vascular pathologies commonly coexist in the brains of elderly individuals.
source: Population-based studies have shown that AD and vascular pathologies commonly coexist in the brains of elderly individuals (Kapasi et al., 2017; Matthews et al., 2009; Neuropathology Group. Medical Research Council Cognitive and Aging, 2001; Rahimi and Kovacs, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to population-based studies.

claim: Atherosclerosis affects as many as up to 60% of all individuals after the age of 55.
source: A major cardiovascular pathology that affects as many as up to 60% of all individuals after the age of 55 is atherosclerosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiology of atherosclerosis, likely drawn from established knowledge.

claim: Atherosclerosis is the progressive thickening, hardening and narrowing of major arteries, including those that supply the brain, such as the carotids.
source: Atherosclerosis is the progressive thickening, hardening and narrowing of major arteries, including those that supply the brain, such as the carotids (Lusis, 2000).
evidence: This is a definition of atherosclerosis supported by a citation.

claim: Intracranial atherosclerosis does not occur until much later in life, around 75 years and above.
source: Intracranial atherosclerosis does not occur until much later in life, around 75 years and above.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of intracranial atherosclerosis development.

claim: Alzheimer's disease that begins around the 8th decade of life is usually present with other comorbidities such as atherosclerosis.
source: As such, Alzheimer's disease that begins around the 8th decade of life is usually present with other comorbidities such as atherosclerosis (Napoli et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Vascular disease and neurovascular unit changes may contribute to AD.
source: There is also evidence that, not only do these often exist as comorbidities, but they may interact pathogenically with vascular disease and neurovascular unit changes contributing to AD (Iadecola, 2017; Kapasi and Schneider, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There are very limited models of comorbidity with respect to preclinical studies.
source: To date, there are very limited models of comorbidity with respect to preclinical studies, and instead models have been very specific and 'pure', and not reflective of the clinical pathology in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of preclinical research models.

claim: Preclinical models have been very specific and 'pure', and not reflective of the clinical pathology in humans.
source: To date, there are very limited models of comorbidity with respect to preclinical studies, and instead models have been very specific and 'pure', and not reflective of the clinical pathology in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current preclinical models.

claim: Atherosclerosis is known to be a major risk factor for the development of dementia.
source: Atherosclerosis is known to be a major risk factor for the development of dementia.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about atherosclerosis as a risk factor.

claim: Progressive atheromatous plaque build-up within cerebral arteries can lead to stenosis producing insufficient oxygen delivery to the brain parenchyma.
source: The progressive atheromatous plaque build-up within cerebral arteries that supply the cortex over time can lead to stenosis producing insufficient oxygen delivery to the brain parenchyma, potentially resulting in neuronal death and symptoms of dementia (Shabir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about atherosclerosis pathophysiology.

claim: Stenosis from atheromatous plaque build-up can potentially result in neuronal death and symptoms of dementia.
source: The progressive atheromatous plaque build-up within cerebral arteries that supply the cortex over time can lead to stenosis producing insufficient oxygen delivery to the brain parenchyma, potentially resulting in neuronal death and symptoms of dementia (Shabir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Vascular cognitive impairment may be attributed to a variety of different vascular pathologies affecting either systemic or intracranial vasculature.
source: Indeed, the vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) which precedes the onset of dementia may be attributed to a variety of different vascular pathologies affecting either systemic or intracranial vasculature (both large or small vessels) (Iadecola et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The breakdown of NVC is thought to be an important and early pathogenic mechanism in the onset and progression of a range of neurological conditions.
source: The breakdown of NVC is thought to be an important and early pathogenic mechanism in the onset and progression of a range of neurological conditions (Zlokovic, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The PCSK9 atherosclerosis model utilises a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) i.v. injection of a gain-of-function mutation (D377Y) to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.
source: We used a novel model of atherosclerosis that utilises a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) i.v. injection of a gain-of-function mutation (D377Y) to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (rAAV8-mPCSK9-D377Y), combined with a high-fat Western diet to induce atherosclerosis in most adult mouse strains (Bjørklund et al., 2014; Roche-Molina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental model used, supported by citations.

claim: The PCSK9 model combined with a high-fat Western diet induces atherosclerosis in most adult mouse strains.
source: We used a novel model of atherosclerosis that utilises a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) i.v. injection of a gain-of-function mutation (D377Y) to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (rAAV8-mPCSK9-D377Y), combined with a high-fat Western diet to induce atherosclerosis in most adult mouse strains (Bjørklund et al., 2014; Roche-Molina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the model.

claim: The PCSK9 model leads to constitutively active inhibition of the LDL-receptor preventing cholesterol internalisation and degradation by hepatocytes.
source: This leads to the constitutively active inhibition of the LDL-receptor preventing cholesterol internalisation and degradation by hepatocytes, leading to hypercholesterolaemia to occur and the development of robust atherosclerotic lesions within 6–8 weeks (Bjørklund et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of the PCSK9 model and is supported by a citation.

claim: The PCSK9 model leads to hypercholesterolaemia and the development of robust atherosclerotic lesions within 6–8 weeks.
source: This leads to the constitutively active inhibition of the LDL-receptor preventing cholesterol internalisation and degradation by hepatocytes, leading to hypercholesterolaemia to occur and the development of robust atherosclerotic lesions within 6–8 weeks (Bjørklund et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the model's timeline.

claim: The J20-hAPP mouse model of fAD over-expresses human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP) with the Swedish (K670N and M671L) and the Indiana (V7171F) familial mutations.
source: The J20-hAPP mouse model of fAD over-expresses human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP) with the Swedish (K670N and M671L) and the Indiana (V7171F) familial mutations (Mucke et al., 2000), which begin to develop amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques around 5–6 months of age, and show signs of cognitive impairments from 4 months (Ameen-Ali et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the J20 mouse model supported by citations.

claim: J20-hAPP mice begin to develop amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques around 5–6 months of age.
source: The J20-hAPP mouse model of fAD over-expresses human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP) with the Swedish (K670N and M671L) and the Indiana (V7171F) familial mutations (Mucke et al., 2000), which begin to develop amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques around 5–6 months of age, and show signs of cognitive impairments from 4 months (Ameen-Ali et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the J20 model characteristics.

claim: J20-hAPP mice show signs of cognitive impairments from 4 months.
source: The J20-hAPP mouse model of fAD over-expresses human amyloid precursor protein (hAPP) with the Swedish (K670N and M671L) and the Indiana (V7171F) familial mutations (Mucke et al., 2000), which begin to develop amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques around 5–6 months of age, and show signs of cognitive impairments from 4 months (Ameen-Ali et al., 2019).

claim: There were no significant alterations to evoked-haemodynamics in the J20-AD model at 9–12 months of age.

claim: Under acute imaging sessions where an electrode was inserted into the brain, J20-AD mice showed significantly perturbed haemodynamics.
source: We have previously reported no significant alterations to evoked-haemodynamics in the J20-AD model of the same age (9–12 m); however, under acute imaging sessions where an electrode was inserted into the brain, we found significantly perturbed haemodynamics (Sharp et al., 2020).

claim: Electrode insertion causes cortical spreading depression (CSD).

claim: Migraine with aura is linked with cardiovascular disease.

source: We report that experimentally induced atherosclerosis in the J20-AD model increased the number of Aβ plaques by 300%.

source: 2D-optical imaging spectroscopy (2D-OIS) measures brain cortical haemodynamics through a thinned cranial window
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

source: J20-AD mice and J20-PCSK9-MIX mice did not exhibit a significant change in HbT across all stimulation conditions compared to WT mice.

source: The largest reduction in HbT post-CSD occurred in J20-AD mice, followed by PCSK9-ATH mice, then J20-PCSK9-MIX mice compared to WT controls.

claim: The significantly different evoked-HbT in PCSK9-ATH mice was due to neurovascular breakdown.

claim: Vascular reactivity was not impaired in any of the mice.

claim: Cerebral arterioles were unaffected by atherosclerosis at 9–12 months.

claim: Cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral blood flow was preserved in the Tg-SwDI model of Alzheimer's.

claim: Electrode insertion causes a cortical spreading depression (CSD) to occur in all animals.
source: As we showed in our previous reports (Shabir et al., 2020; Sharp et al., 2020), the technical procedure of electrode insertion causes a cortical spreading depression (CSD) to occur in all animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and current observations.

claim: CSD has two distinct phases: a wave of depolarisation within the grey matter and haemodynamic changes.
source: CSD has two distinct phases: (1) a wave of depolarisation within the grey matter characterised by neuronal distortion leading to a large change of the membrane potential whereby neuronal activity is silenced (spreading depression) and (2) haemodynamic changes that accompany neuronal spreading depolarisation which typically result in a wave of prolonged reduced perfusion that persists for some time (Ayata and Lauritzen, 2015; Dreier, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of CSD supported by citations.

claim: CSD does not typically occur in healthy brain tissue.
source: CSD does not typically occur in healthy brain tissue, however, it is a common neurophysiological occurrence in certain pathological conditions including migraine, epilepsy, brain injury, hyperthermia, hypoxia, and ischaemia (Dreier, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSD supported by a citation.

claim: CSD is a common neurophysiological occurrence in certain pathological conditions including migraine, epilepsy, brain injury, hyperthermia, hypoxia, and ischaemia.
source: CSD does not typically occur in healthy brain tissue, however, it is a common neurophysiological occurrence in certain pathological conditions including migraine, epilepsy, brain injury, hyperthermia, hypoxia, and ischaemia (Dreier, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSD supported by a citation.

claim: In WT mice, the initial reduction in HbT during CSD is small, and a robust haemodynamic recovery occurs.
source: In WT mice, the initial reduction in HbT is small, and a robust haemodynamic recovery occurs which allows for neurovascular coupling to occur to sustain neurons metabolically.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of CSD in WT mice.

claim: Diseased animals exhibit a large reduction in HbT during CSD with an extremely limited haemodynamic recovery resulting in prolonged constriction, severe reductions to blood volume and HbO and HbR levels indicating hypoxia and ischaemia.
source: This is a marked difference to the diseased animals, which upon electrode insertion to cause a CSD, exhibit a large reduction in HbT with an extremely limited haemodynamic recovery resulting in a prolonged constriction, severe reductions to blood volume and HbO and HbR levels indicating hypoxia and ischaemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of CSD in diseased mice.

claim: The haemodynamic response to CSD in diseased mice is severely inappropriate and can lead to long lasting devastating effects such as widespread cortical pannecrosis of neurons and astrocytes.
source: Thus, the haemodynamic response to CSD in diseased mice is severely inappropriate and can lead to long lasting devastating effects such as widespread cortical pannecrosis of neurons and astrocytes (Dreier, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference about potential consequences supported by a citation.

claim: Baseline blood volumes do not recover in the diseased animals for a much longer period compared to WT animals.
source: As our data show, baseline blood volumes do not recover in the diseased animals for a much longer period compared to WT animals, with the most profound CSD occurring in J20-AD mice, followed by PCSK9-ATH mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on CSD recovery.

claim: The most profound CSD occurs in J20-AD mice, followed by PCSK9-ATH mice.
source: As our data show, baseline blood volumes do not recover in the diseased animals for a much longer period compared to WT animals, with the most profound CSD occurring in J20-AD mice, followed by PCSK9-ATH mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on CSD severity.

claim: CSD may be the neuropathological link between migraine, stroke, cardiovascular disease and dementia.
source: CSD may be the neuropathological link between migraine, stroke, cardiovascular disease and dementia in which cardiovascular risk factors, genetics and other lifestyle factors which prime the onset of migraine to occur lead to vascular vulnerability within the brain predisposing affected individuals to an increased risk of cerebral ischaemia and haemorrhagic stroke (Ripa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Shared genetic and associated clinical features observed in migraine patients are involved in the increased vulnerability to cerebral ischaemia.
source: There is accumulating evidence to suggest that shared genetic and associated clinical features observed in migraine patients are involved in the increased vulnerability to cerebral ischaemia, therefore, predisposing affected individuals to stroke and white matter lesions associated with dementia (Yemisci and Eikermann-Haerter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Mouse models of CADASIL have enhanced CSD linking a dysfunctional neurovascular unit with migraine with aura.
source: Indeed, mouse models of cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy syndrome (CADASIL); a genetic cerebrovascular disease caused by NOTCH3 mutations that has a high frequency of migraines with aura, have enhanced CSD linking a dysfunctional neurovascular unit with migraine with aura (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on CADASIL mouse models.

claim: Women who suffered from migraines with aura had a higher incidence rate of cardiovascular disease compared to women without aura or any migraines.
source: Furthermore, a recent study examined women who suffered from migraines with and without aura and found that those that suffered migraines with aura had a higher incidence rate of cardiovascular disease compared to women without aura or any migraines (Kurth et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Migraine history was positively associated with an increased risk of developing both all-cause dementia and AD, but not VaD.
source: In addition, another recent study found that migraine history was positively associated with an increased risk of developing both all-cause dementia and AD, but not VaD (Morton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Systemic disease can prime the brain to allow profound CSDs to occur in the context of migraine.
source: Our study, along with the previously discussed studies provide an explanation for these recent findings and highlights how systemic disease can prime the brain to allow profound CSDs to occur in the context of migraine, and as such, migraine frequency and intensity may be related to the onset of neurological disease by later in life including dementia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study and cited literature.

claim: Migraine frequency and intensity may be related to the onset of neurological disease later in life including dementia.
source: Our study, along with the previously discussed studies provide an explanation for these recent findings and highlights how systemic disease can prime the brain to allow profound CSDs to occur in the context of migraine, and as such, migraine frequency and intensity may be related to the onset of neurological disease by later in life including dementia.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current study and cited literature.

claim: PCSK9-ATH mice display consistently reduced evoked-HbT responses against evoked MUA compared to WT controls.
source: A consistent finding irrespective of stimulation and condition was that PCSK9-ATH mice display consistently reduced evoked-HbT responses against evoked MUA (observed in chronic and acute experiments respectively) compared to WT controls, which suggests an advanced level of neurovascular breakdown and inefficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduced evoked-HbT responses in PCSK9-ATH mice suggest an advanced level of neurovascular breakdown and inefficiency.
source: A consistent finding irrespective of stimulation and condition was that PCSK9-ATH mice display consistently reduced evoked-HbT responses against evoked MUA (observed in chronic and acute experiments respectively) compared to WT controls, which suggests an advanced level of neurovascular breakdown and inefficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neurovascular coupling data.

claim: When breathing air, PCSK9-ATH and J20-PCSK9-ATH mice could be hypoxic and have a metabolic deficit.
source: This is further supported by the whisker stimulation data while animals breathed air (21% oxygen) where HbR is inverted in PCSK9-ATH and J20-PCSK9-ATH mice (Figure 2); as such, when breathing air the mice could be hypoxic and have a metabolic deficit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the HbR data.

claim: Other groups have found similarly reduced blood flow in the ApoE-/- model without altered cortical activation.
source: Other groups have found similarly reduced blood flow in the ApoE-/- model without altered cortical activation (Ayata et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to another study.

source: A recent study found decreased tissue oxygenation in the LDLR-/- mouse model of atherosclerosis (Li et al., 2019), and this is most likely to be the case in the PCSK9 model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Decreased tissue oxygenation is most likely to be the case in the PCSK9 model.
source: A recent study found decreased tissue oxygenation in the LDLR-/- mouse model of atherosclerosis (Li et al., 2019), and this is most likely to be the case in the PCSK9 model.

source: However, haemodynamic responses to later stimulations matched those of WT mice, confirming the non-significant effect of disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute imaging sessions.

claim: Neurovascular measures in PCSK9-ATH mice remained consistently impaired compared to WT throughout the whole experimental period.
source: Throughout the whole experimental period, neurovascular measures in PCSK9-ATH mice remained consistently impaired compared to WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: While CSD has a profound effect on stimulation-evoked haemodynamic responses in all disease groups, time allows for recovery for WT, J20-AD and J20-PCSK9-MIX groups, but PCSK9-ATH mice are still affected due to genuine long-lasting neurovascular deficits.
source: Together, these data indicate that whilst CSD has a profound effect on stimulation-evoked haemodynamic responses in all disease groups, time allows for recovery for WT, J20-AD and J20-PCSK9-MIX groups, but PCSK9-ATH; despite being recovered, are still affected due to genuine long-lasting neurovascular deficits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data across all groups.

source: Angiogenesis is known to be triggered in cerebral microvessels in AD in response to increased Aβ and neuroinflammation and may initially reflect a compensatory mechanism to increase perfusion (Jefferies et al., 2013).
